description: We aim to identify and study locations on Earth that resemble potential sites for permanent human bases on the Moon and Mars. By comparing extreme environments, geological features, temperatures, and available resources, we hope to understand how Earth can serve as a testing ground for future space exploration.
summary: The Summary of Analog Atlas is it shows the places on earth and compares them to places on the Moon and Mars. Then using a code with 5 different variables we compare places on Mars and the Moon to Earth to rank their similarities out of 100. The 5 Variables being: Temperature, Steepness, Dryness, Rockiness and Roughness.
details:
Project Details

What it does
Analog Atlas finds places on Earth that are most like the Moon and Mars. Astronauts, rovers and equipment are tested on Earth before they go to space. The well-known analog sites have already been studied a lot, and no single place on Earth matches the Moon or Mars completely. We wanted to find less-studied analogs and show exactly where each one matches and where it doesn’t.

How it works
We picked 15 Earth sites. Some are classic analogs (Craters of the Moon, Lanzarote, Namib Desert, Askja). Others are less-studied (Bozjyra Valley & Ustyurt Plateau in Kazakhstan, Deosai Plains in Pakistan, Al-Qarah Caves in Saudi Arabia, Al-Wusta Gravel Peneplain in Oman, Tsingy de Bemaraha in Madagascar). We compared each site to Mars and Moon target values on 5 variables:

  • Temperature (°C)
  • Steepness / slope (°)
  • Dryness (0 to 1)
  • Rockiness (0 to 1)
  • Roughness (0 to 1)

Our Python code in Google Colab gives each site a score for every variable. It then combines those into one similarity score out of 100 and ranks the sites. The Mars target is -63°C, 5° slope, dryness 1.0, rockiness 0.80 and roughness 0.55. The Moon target is -50°C, 10° slope, dryness 1.0, rockiness 0.95 and roughness 0.65.

Results

  • Mars top 3: Bozjyra/Ustyurt (81.5%), Askja Pumice Fields (76.9%), Pingualuit Crater (73.4%)
  • Moon top 3: Craters of the Moon (83.9%), Askja (83.3%), Tolbachik/Kamchatka (77.9%)

The surprise was Askja: it came 2nd for both the Moon and Mars. Our #1 Mars match, Bozjyra, is barely used as an analog. Its wind-eroded layered cliffs are good for testing how rovers drive, climb and drill.

The website
Our website lets anyone switch between Mars and the Moon and change how much each variable counts. The ranking updates live, so a mission team can focus on what matters for its test. For example, a wheel test would weight roughness more and a thermal test would weight temperature more.

Limitations (what Earth can’t copy)
Earth can’t copy vacuum, low gravity, radiation or the absence of life. Some site values are our own estimates, not measurements, so the scores are a starting guide and not a final scientific result.

Tools
Python, Google Colab, a JavaScript website hosted on Vercel, and Canva for the presentation.

Why it matters / next steps
Testing at more varied analog sites helps NASA and other agencies catch problems before a mission instead of during one. Next, we want to build a searchable global map with more sites and more variables, using real satellite measurements for every value.

Team
Lunar Regolith (Jordan, Zohan, Aeson), ages 13 to 15.
